newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Prominent North Korean defector shot near Seoul.
newsitem.headline: Prominent North Korean defector shot near Seoul.

text.p: Two suspected North Korean agents shot and seriously wounded a defector who is a relative of Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il's ex-wife, police said on Sunday.
The South Korean government called an emergency meeting of security-related ministers to discuss the attack later on Sunday, officials said.

Senior Superintendent Kim Choong-nam, who is heading a police probe into the attack, said Li Il-nam was in critical condition after being shot near Seoul late on Saturday by the two men armed with Belgian-made Browning pistols.
"We have several clues for the case pointing to North Korea," he told Reuters.

He said he suspected Pyongyang had ordered the gunmen to attack Li as a warning to both the Seoul government and defectors after the defection of a high-ranking North Korean official now marooned in the South Korean mission in Beijing.
Tensions on the divided Korean peninsula have flared since Wednesday, when Hwang Jang-yop, a senior adviser to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, arrived by taxi at the South's embassy in China.

South Korea says Hwang is seeking asylum in the South, while a furious North Korea insists he was kidnapped. Hwang, ranked 24th in the Stalinist state's hierarchy, would be the most senior Pyongyang official to seek asylum in the South.
Senior Superintendent Kim said Li, known in South Korea as Lee Han-yong, is the nephew of Sung Hye-rim, former wife of Kim Jong-il, who celebrates his 55th birthday on Sunday.
Li, 36, was shot outside his temporary home at Bundang, just south of Seoul, Kim said. "Li told witnesses 'spy, spy' before he went unconscious."
He said North Korean agents had frequently used Browning pistols for terrorist attacks in the past.
Officials at a nearby hospital said surgery on the defector could not remove a bullet in his head as it was too deeply lodged. Li remained unconscious.
Police officers said neighbour Park Chong-un saw Li lying outside his apartment and reported the incident to police.
Park and Nam Sang-hwa, who lived in the same apartment as Li, witnessed the attack through video monitoring devices from their homes, they said.
Police believed the attackers used silencers as neighbours heard no gunshots. An analysis of two used cartridges at the scene showed the weapons used were Browning pistols.
The attack took place as China agonised over what to do with Hwang, a top Pyongyang ideologue who is a member of the powerful secretariat of the North's ruling Workers' (Communist) Party.

Allowing Hwang to go to Seoul, where he could be expected to reveal crucial secrets about the North Korean state, would offend Beijing's old communist comrades, while sending him back to Pyongyang would endanger China's ties with its new capitalist friend, which has already proved a valuable investor.

Hwang's apparent betrayal has caused a massive loss of face for a North Korean government already reeling from severe food shortages and economic disasters. Fearing retaliation, Seoul has ordered tighter security at all its overseas missions.
Police in Seoul and surrounding Kyonggi Province have been placed on alert since the attack on Li and a search is under way for the gunmen.

Li, who came to South Korea in the early 1980s from Europe where he had been studying, is the first North Korean defector to be shot in the South since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War, according to police.
Despite the 1953 truce, the two Koreas have remained implacable foes and their tense common border, bristling with advanced weapons, is today the last Cold War frontier.
